la:noun:auspicium.html:
auspĭcĭum, ii, n.
auspex
,
divination by observing the flight of birds, augury from birds, auspices (cf. augurium).
Lit.: auspicia avium, (as if overlooking the origin of auspicium): praetor auspicat auspicium prosperum, Naev. ap. : Dant (Romulus et Remus) operam simul auspicio augurioque etc., Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 81 sq. Vahl.: pullarium in auspicium mittit,: ab auspicio bono proficisci, of marriage, Ellis (cf. auspex, II. A. 2.) et saep.; cf. the class. passages,; sq.; —So auspicium habere, to have the right of taking auspices (which, in the performance of civil duties, was possessed by all magistrates, but, in time of war, only by the commander - in - chief): omnes magistratus auspicium judiciumque habento,: quod nemo plebeius auspicia haberet,.—Of the commander - in - chief: expugnatum oppidumst Imperio atque auspicio mei eri Amphitruonis,: Ut gesserit rem publicam ductu, imperio, auspicio suo,; 2, 2, 25: qui ductu auspicioque ejus res prospere gesserant,; ; ; 41, 28, 1 al.; 21, 40, 3: recepta signa ductu Germanici, auspiciis Tiberii,: Septentrionalis oceanus navigatus est auspiciis divi Augusti,: alia ductu meo, alia imperio auspicioque perdomui,: domuit partim ductu partim auspiciis suis Cantabriam, etc., Ruhnk.—And so absol.: vates rege vatis habenas, Auspicio felix totus ut annus eat (sc. tuo), Merk.—Hence for the chief command, guidance: tuis auspiciis totum confecta duella per orbem, Schmid: Illius auspiciis obsessae moenia pacem Victa petent Mutinae,.—And, in gen., right, power, inclination, will: Me si fata meis paterentur ducere vitam Auspiciis et sponte meā componere curas, etc.,: Communem hunc ergo populum paribusque regamus Auspiciis, (aequali potestate, Serv.).—
Transf., in gen., a sign, omen, a divine premonition or token: Liquido exeo auspicio foras, Avi sinistrā,; so : optimum,: dicere ausus est optimis auspiciis ea geri, : quae contra rem publicam ferrentur, contra auspicia ferri,: melius,: vanum,: infaustum,: felix,—So, auspicium facere, of things which give signs, tokens, omens: augurium haec (mustela) facit,: cur aliis a laevā, aliis a dexterā datum est avibus, ut ratum auspicium facere possint?: circa summum culmen hominis auspicium fecisse,.—Poet.: cui (diviti) si vitiosa libido Fecerit auspicium, gave him a token (viz. for changing), urged him to a new decision, Hor, Ep. 1, 1, 86.—
Trop., = initium, a beginning (cf. auspicor, II., and auspex, II. B.): auspicia belli a parricidio incipientes,: auspicia regni a parricidio coepit,.

la:noun:auspex.html:
auspex, spĭcis, comm.
a contraction of avispex, from avis-spicio
,
a bird inspector, bird-seer, i. e. one who observes the flight, singing, or feeding of birds, and foretells future events therefrom; an augur, soothsayer, diviner (in a lit. signif. far more rare than augur).
Lit.: latores et auspices legis curiatae,: ego cui timebo Providus auspex,.—Of the birds from which auguries were taken: (galli, gallinacei) victoriarum omnium auspices,.—Since little of importance was done in Rome without consulting the auspices, hence,
Transf.
In gen., an author, founder, director, leader, protector, favorer: divis Auspicibus coeptorum operum,: Dis equidem auspicibus reor etc.,, and : auspice Musā, i. e. under the inspiration of the muse, 1, 3, 13: Nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro,.—
Esp., as t. t., the person who witnessed the marriage contract, the reception of the marriage portion, took care that the marriage ceremonies were rightly performed, etc., παρανύμφιος: nihil fere quondam majoris rei nisi auspicato ne privatim quidem gerebatur, quod etiam nunc nuptiarum auspices declarant, qui re omissā nomen tantum tenent,; cf. ; ; : nubit genero socrus nullis auspicibus, nullis auctoribus, etc.,; so : auspicum verba,; : alicui nubere dote inter auspices consignatā,; veniet cum signatoribus auspex, Schol.; Schol.—In fem., ; cf. pronubus; auctor, II. F. 3.; and Smith, Dict. Antiq.—
A beginning (post-class.), ; .—
Adj., fortunate, favorable, auspicious, lucky (post-class.): clamor,: victoria,: purpura,.

la:verb:auspicor.html:
auspĭcor, ātus, 1, v. dep.
from auspex, as auguror from augur
,
to take the auspices.
Lit.
In gen.: (Gracchus) cum pomerium transiret, auspicari esset oblitus,: tripudio auspicari,; : Fabio auspicanti aves non addixere,; ; sq. al.—
Esp., aliquid or absol., also with inf., to make a beginning, for the sake of a good omen, to begin, enter upon (first freq. after the Aug. per.): ipsis Kal. Januariis auspicandi causā omne genus operis instaurant,: auspicandi gratiā tribunal ingredi,: non auspicandi causā, sed studendi,: auspicatus est et jurisdictionem,: auspicabar in Virginem (aquam) desilire,.—
In gen., to begin, enter upon a thing: auspicari culturarum officia,; : homo a suppliciis vitam auspicatur,, prooem. § 3: militiam,: cantare,.— Trop.: senatorium per militiam auspicantes gradum,attaining, receiving it through military services,.!*?
Act. access. form auspĭco, āre, to take the auspices: praetor advenit, auspicat auspicium prosperum, (Non. p 468, 28): (magistratus) publicae [rei] cum auspicant, Caecil. ap. Non. l. l. (Com. Rel. p. 66 Rib.): auspicetis: cras est communis dies, Atta, ib. (Com. Rel. p. 161 Rib.): Non hodie isti rei auspicavi,: mustelam,to receive, accept as an augury,: super aliquā re,. —
Pass.
Abl. absol.: auspĭcātō, after taking the auspices: Romulus non solum auspicato urbem condidisse, sed ipse etiam optimus augur fuisse traditur,: Nihil fere quondam majoris rei nisi auspicato ne privatim quidem gerebatur,: qui et consul rogari et augur et auspicato,; ; : plebeius magistratus nullus auspicato creatur,; ; ; 28, 28: Hunc (senatum) auspicato a parente et conditore urbis nostrae institutum,; —
auspĭcātus, a, um, part., consecrated by auguries: auspicato in loco,: non auspicatos contudit impetus Nostros,: auspicata comitia,—
Acc. to auspicor, II., begun: in bello male auspicato,. —
auspĭcātus, a, um, as P. a., fortunate, favorable, lucky, prosperous, auspicious: cum Liviam auspicatis rei publicae ominibus duxisset uxorem,.— Comp.: Venus auspicatior,: arbor,.—Sup.: auspicatissimum exordium,; : initium,.—Adv.: auspĭcātō, under a good omen, auspiciously: ut ingrediare auspicato,at a for tunate moment, in a lucky hour,: Haud auspicato huc me appuli,: qui auspicato a Chelidone surrexisset,.—Comp. auspicatius: auspicatius mutare nomen,: gigni,.

la:adj:austerus.html:
austērus, a, um, adj. (auster, ;
sup. austerrimus, Messala, Corv. Progen. Aug. 5), = αὐστηρός.
Lit, of taste, harsh, sour, tart (not before the Aug. per.; syn.: acer, acerbus, tristis, severus, molestus): vinum nigrum,: austerior gustus,: herba austero sapore,: vinum austerissimum,.—
Transf. *
Of smell, pungent: balsami sucus: odore austerus,.—
Of color, deep, dark: sunt autem colores austeri aut floridi,.—Comp.: (pictor) austerior colore et in austeritate jucundior,.—
Trop.
Severe, rigid, strict, stern, austere (opp. mol lis, facilis, lenis; scarcely before Cic.): illo austero more ac modo,; : austerior et gravior esse potuisset,: Nec gravis austeri poena cavenda viri,: homo austerus es,; .—Of discourse, severe, grave, serious: ita sit noLis ornatus et suavis orator, ut suavitatem habeat austeram et solidam, non dulcem atque decoctam (the epithet borrowed from wine),that he may have a severe and solid, not a luscious and effeminate sweetness,: austera poëmata,: oratio, Spald.—Of style in statuary: genus,.—
As the opp. of kind, pleasant, severe, gloomy, sad, troublesome, hard, irksome (so first after the beginning of the Aug. per.): labor,: Quaelibet austeras de me ferat urna tabellas,: aeger omnem austeram curationem recusans,.—Adv.:

la:verb:ausculto.html:
ausculto, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. freq. [perh. a union of two roots, that of audio, auris ausis, and of the Sanscr. çru = to hear; v. Bopp, Gloss. p. 396 b.], to hear any person or thing with attention, to listen to, give ear to, ἀκροᾶσθαι (cf. audio init.; in the anteclass. per. freq., but not in Lucr.; in the class. per. rare).
In gen.: Ita est cupidus orationis, ut conducat qui auscultet, Cato ap. : ausculto atque animum adverto sedulo,: In rem quod sit praevortaris quam re advorsā animo auscultes,; ; : nimis eum ausculto libens,; : Ausculta paucis, nisi molestumst,; and 5: jam scies: Ausculta, (9), 7: illos ausculto lubens, Afran. ap : Nec populum auscultare, * : sermonem,: verba,: aures diligenter auscultabunt, ib. Isa, 32, 3.—
Esp
To listen to something believingly, to give credit to, etc.
With acc.: crimina,.—
With dat. of pers.: cui auscultabant,gave heed,.—
To listen in secret to something, to overhear: quid habeat sermonis, auscultabo,: omnia ego istaec auscultavi ab ostio,.—
Of servants, to attend or wait at the door, as in Gr. ὑπακούειν: ad fores auscultato atque serva has aedīs,: jam dudum ausculto et cupiens tibi dicere servus Pauca, reformido, * Heind.—
Alicui or absol., to hear obediently, to obey, heed (cf. audio): hi auscultare dicuntur, qui auditis parent, Müll.: auscultare est obsequi: audire ignoti quod imperant soleo, non auscultare,: magis audiendum quam auscultandum censeo, Pac. ap. : Age nunc vincito me auscultato filio,: Qui mi auscultabunt,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : seni auscultare,: vin tu homini stulto mi auscultare?; ; : mihi ausculta: vide, ne tibi desis, * .—With acc.: nisi me

auscultas, (we should perhaps here, in accordance with the general idiom, read mi; so Ritschl).—In pass. impers.: De. Ad portum ne bitas, dico jam tibi. Ch. Auscultabitur, you shall be obeyed, it shall be done, .!*? It is difficult to believe, in the verse of Afranius, videt ludos, hinc auscultavi procul, that auscultare is equivalent to videre, spectare, acc. to .
